system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2133-11-27 22:51:00 to 2133-11-30 14:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with HCV- and alcohol-related cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and chronic depression was admitted for severe hyperglycemia (glucose 802) and abdominal pain with hematochezia. She was diagnosed with hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state and treated with IV fluids and an insulin drip, later transitioning to subcutaneous insulin. Her abdominal pain was chronic and possibly exacerbated by metabolic derangements, with hematochezia attributed to hemorrhoids. CT imaging showed stable cirrhosis and no acute intra-abdominal pathology. She improved with treatment, her kidney function normalized, and she was discharged home on a new insulin regimen with close follow-up. A severe headache on discharge day prompted a head CT, which was normal. She remains committed to sobriety despite psychosocial stressors.
problems: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with hyperosmolarity without nonketotic hyperglycemic-hyperosmolar coma (NKHHC)
Alcoholic cirrhosis of liver without ascites
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified
Other diseases of stomach and duodenum
Encounter for examination for normal comparison and control in clinical research program

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:   ___ with confusion  // ?PNA

TECHNIQUE:  Single portable view of the chest.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS: 

There are linear bibasilar opacities likely due to atelectasis.  The lungs are
otherwise grossly clear within limitation of relatively low lung volumes.  The
cardiomediastinal silhouette is within normal limits.  No acute osseous
abnormalities.

IMPRESSION: 

Bibasilar atelectasis without definite acute cardiopulmonary process.

EXAMINATION:  CT HEAD W/O CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ woman with altered mental status.  Evaluate for
hemorrhage.

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous axial images of the brain were obtained without
contrast. Coronal and sagittal reformations as well as bone algorithm
reconstructions were provided and reviewed.

DOSE:  Total DLP (Head) = 803 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  Head CT dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

No evidence of infarction, hemorrhage, edema, or mass.  The ventricles and
sulci are normal in size and configuration.

No evidence of fracture.  The visualized portion of the paranasal sinuses,
mastoid air cells, and middle ear cavities are essentially clear.  The
visualized portion of the orbits are unremarkable.

IMPRESSION: 

No acute intracranial abnormality, no hemorrhage.

EXAMINATION:  CT abdomen and pelvis

INDICATION:  ___ woman with abdominal pain and altered mental status. 
Evaluate for diverticulitis.  Per OMR, the patient has a history of HCC with
RFA of a segment II HCC on ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Single phase split bolus contrast: MDCT axial images were acquired
through the abdomen and pelvis following intravenous contrast administration
with split bolus technique.
Oral contrast was not administered.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.

DOSE:  Acquisition sequence:
   1) Stationary Acquisition 6.0 s, 0.5 cm; CTDIvol = 28.9 mGy (Body) DLP =
14.4 mGy-cm.
   2) Spiral Acquisition 5.0 s, 54.5 cm; CTDIvol = 16.3 mGy (Body) DLP = 886.1
mGy-cm.
 Total DLP (Body) = 901 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST:  There is moderate bilateral plate-like linear and basilar
atelectasis.  No evidence of pleural or pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY:  The liver is shrunken and nodular, compatible with cirrhosis. 
A 3.7 x 2.8 cm peripheral hypodensity in segment 2 corresponding to the area
of prior radiofrequency ablation of a HCC, previously measured 3.6 x 2.5 cm
and is overall unchanged (series 2, image 18; series 601 B, image 24).  No new
focal hepatic lesion is identified on this nondedicated exam.  No intrahepatic
biliary ductal dilation.  The common bile duct remains ectatic, measuring up
to 8 mm, previously 11 mm, likely related to prior cholecystectomy.  The
umbilical vein is recanalized. The main, left, and right anterior and
posterior portal veins appear patent.  The splenic vein and SMV also appear
patent.  Collaterals in the anterior abdominal wall are overall unchanged. 
The gallbladder is surgically absent.

PANCREAS: The pancreas has normal attenuation throughout, without evidence of
focal lesions or pancreatic ductal dilatation.  No peripancreatic stranding.

SPLEEN: The spleen remains mildly enlarged, measuring up to 13.8 cm.  No focal
splenic lesion.

ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size and shape.

URINARY: The kidneys are of normal and symmetric size with normal nephrogram. 
Bilateral renal cortical hypodensities are overall unchanged.  No
hydronephrosis or perinephric abnormality.

GASTROINTESTINAL: Esophageal varices are again seen.  The stomach is
unremarkable.  Small bowel loops demonstrate normal caliber, wall thickness,
and enhancement throughout.  The colon and rectum are within normal limits. 
The appendix is normal.  No bowel obstruction.  No drainable intra-abdominal
fluid collection.  No free air.

PELVIS: The urinary bladder is decompressed with a Foley catheter in place and
contains excreted intravenous contrast.  The distal ureters are unremarkable. 
No free fluid in the pelvis.

LYMPH NODES:  Scattered small prominent retroperitoneal lymph nodes are of
uncertain significance but could be reactive. No mesenteric lymphadenopathy. 
No pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

VASCULAR: No abdominal aortic aneurysm.  Moderate atherosclerotic disease is
noted.

BONES: No evidence of worrisome osseous lesions or acute fracture.  Mild
levoconvex scoliosis of the lumbar spine is unchanged.  Left pubic ramus
fractures with callus formation and ___.  Associated small chronic soft
tissue changes with calcifications, possibly old hematoma are unchanged. 
Chronic changes in the sacrum.

SOFT TISSUES: The abdominal and pelvic wall is within normal limits other than
collaterals.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  No acute intra-abdominal or pelvic process.

2.  Cirrhosis with sequela of portal hypertension with splenomegaly and
esophageal varices.

3.  Post RFA changes in segment 2, overall similar CT appearance to the prior
exam but this exam is not dedicated to evaluate hepatic masses.

4.  No diverticulosis.

EXAMINATION:  DUPLEX DOPP ABD/PEL

INDICATION:  eval for biliary dilatation, portal vein thrombosis

TECHNIQUE:  Gray scale, color, and spectral Doppler evaluation of the abdomen
was performed.  As per discussion with the ordering team, the study was
tailored exclusively to doppler evaluation.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal/pelvic CT from ___.

FINDINGS: 

The liver shows a coarsened echotexture and nodular contour in keeping with
cirrhosis.

Doppler evaluation:

The main portal vein is patent, with flow in the appropriate direction.
Main portal vein velocity is 26.3 cm/sec.
Right portal vein, including the anterior and posterior branches, as well as
the left portal vein are patent, with adequate direction of flow.

The main hepatic artery is patent, with appropriate waveform.
Right, middle and left hepatic veins are patent, with appropriate waveforms.
Splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein are patent, with antegrade flow.
The IVC is patent.
Note is made of a recannalized paraumbilical vein with hepatopetal flow.

IMPRESSION: 

Patent hepatic vasculature.  Findings consistent with hepatic cirrhosis with
sequelae of portal hypertension including recanalization of the paraumbilical
vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the hospital because your daughters called EMS when you were confused at home. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I don’t really know. I was at home and my girls said I wasn’t making sense. I just felt foggy. I’m sorry, I can’t think straight right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. You’re safe now. We’re trying to figure out why this happened. You have cirrhosis from hepatitis C and past alcohol use, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. And liver cancer, but I’ve had treatments for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we see you’ve had RFA and TACE. Right now, your confusion makes us think you might have hepatic encephalopathy — that’s when the liver isn’t clearing toxins well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I’ve had that before. But I’ve been taking my rifaximin. I just… I stopped the lactulose. I don’t like how it makes me feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be exactly why you got confused. Lactulose helps clear ammonia from your system. We’re going to restart it every two hours to help you clear your mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I know… I just hate the cramps and the bathroom trips. But if it helps, I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you closely. We also did some tests — a CT scan of your head and abdomen, and your labs. The good news is no bleeding, stroke, or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No stroke? I was so scared. And my belly pain — is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your belly pain is in the right upper side, where your liver is. The CT shows your cirrhosis is stable, no new issues. The pain may be from your liver swelling a bit or just chronic discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver cancer? Is it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan isn’t detailed enough to check the tumor closely, but the area treated before looks stable. We’ll follow up with your liver doctor for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… thank you. I’ve been so stressed. My daughter has cancer too. It’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry to hear that. That’s a lot to carry. We’ll make sure you have support. For now, let’s focus on getting your mind clear and your body stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your liver enzymes are a bit high — AST and ALT — but not alarming. Your blood count is low, but that’s your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there infection? I’ve been worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. Your blood cultures came back clean, and your white count is low but stable. We also checked for CMV — it’s negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the ultrasound they did yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Doppler ultrasound showed your liver blood vessels are open and flowing well. No clots. But it confirmed cirrhosis and portal hypertension, which we already knew.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing new is wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The main issue was the confusion from hepatic encephalopathy, likely because you stopped lactulose. We’re keeping you on it every two hours for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? My sugars have been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was 104 when you came in — not too high. But your A1c is 10.2%, so we know it’s not well controlled. We’ll keep you on your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve had several bowel movements today — that’s good. It means the lactulose is working. How’s your thinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I feel like my head is clearing. I’m still tired, but I can follow things now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to slowly restart your other medications — like quetiapine and gabapentin — now that you’re more alert.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was taking more oxycodone too. My daughter was using my pills — I didn’t know until now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could have made the confusion worse. But we’ve reviewed it — you’re tolerating your usual dose fine now. Just stick to your prescription.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson. No skipping lactulose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs this morning show your liver tests are improving — AST and ALT are coming down. Your mental status is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the headaches I’ve been having?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had migrainous headaches, but no neurological changes. We think you might have been overusing Excedrin at home. That can cause rebound headaches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was taking it a few times a day… I didn’t know that could make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. We’ll recommend you see your doctor for a proper headache workup after discharge. For now, your pain is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Your labs are stable, you’re alert, and you’ve had regular bowel movements. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. But I’m nervous about managing everything at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending a visiting nurse to help with your meds for a few days. And you must keep taking lactulose — it’s key to preventing another episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve seen what happens when I don’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, follow up with your primary doctor and liver specialist. If you get confused again, have severe belly pain, or black stools, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to reach out. We’re here for you.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with HCV- and alcohol-related cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and type 2 diabetes was admitted for acute confusion. She was found to have hepatic encephalopathy, likely due to non-adherence to her lactulose regimen and possible medication overuse, including oxycodone and Excedrin. Initial evaluation showed no acute intracranial, abdominal, or infectious processes on imaging and labs. Her mental status improved with q2h lactulose and temporary hold of sedating medications, which were gradually restarted. Headaches during admission were thought to be medication-overuse related and improved with regimen adjustment. She was discharged home with a visiting nurse for medication support, with instructions to maintain lactulose adherence and follow up with her primary and liver specialists.
